top_level_objectives: Understand the fundamental principles of VSEPR theory.
Predict the electron-domain and molecular geometries of covalent molecules.
Relate molecular geometry to the physical and chemical properties of molecules.
Recognize common molecular geometries and their corresponding idealized and actual bond angles.

scenes.brief_purpose: Introduce the core concept of VSEPR theory: electron pairs repel each other and arrange themselves to minimize this repulsion.
key_visuals: A central atom with several electron pairs (represented as spheres or clouds) around it, initially in a random arrangement.
Visual representation of repulsive forces between electron pairs.
student_actions: Observe the initial random arrangement of electron pairs.
Manipulate the electron pairs to find an arrangement that minimizes repulsion.
Note how the pairs naturally spread apart.

scenes.brief_purpose: Demonstrate the five fundamental electron-domain geometries predicted by VSEPR theory for 2 to 6 electron domains.
key_visuals: Interactive models showing the arrangement of electron domains for 2 (linear), 3 (trigonal planar), 4 (tetrahedral), 5 (trigonal bipyramidal), and 6 (octahedral) electron domains.
Labels identifying each geometry and the associated bond angles.
student_actions: Select the number of electron domains around a central atom.
Observe the resulting electron-domain geometry.
Identify the name of each fundamental geometry.

scenes.scene_name: Predicting Molecular Geometry: No Lone Pairs
scenes.brief_purpose: Illustrate how to determine molecular geometry when there are no lone pairs on the central atom, using examples like methane (CH4).
key_visuals: A central atom bonded to multiple other atoms, with no lone pairs on the central atom.
The electron-domain geometry visually matching the molecular geometry.
Example molecules like CH4 with labeled bond angles.
student_actions: Start with a Lewis structure (e.g., CH4).
Identify the number of electron domains and the electron-domain geometry.
Determine the molecular geometry, which is the same as the electron-domain geometry when there are no lone pairs.
Compare the predicted geometry to the provided example.

scenes.brief_purpose: Explore how lone pairs affect molecular geometry, using examples like water (H2O) and ammonia (NH3).
key_visuals: Central atom with both bonding pairs and lone pairs.
Visual distinction between bonding pairs (connecting atoms) and lone pairs (on the central atom).
The electron-domain geometry (e.g., tetrahedral) and the resulting molecular geometry (e.g., bent for water, trigonal pyramidal for ammonia).
Labels showing idealized vs. actual bond angles.
student_actions: Add lone pairs to the central atom.
Observe how lone pairs influence the arrangement of bonding pairs.
Identify the resulting molecular geometry.
Compare the actual bond angles to the idealized angles and note the effect of lone pairs.

scenes.brief_purpose: Introduce and visualize more complex electron-domain geometries and their derived molecular geometries, including examples with lone pairs.
key_visuals: Interactive models for trigonal bipyramidal and octahedral electron-domain geometries.
Examples of molecules with these electron-domain geometries that have lone pairs (e.g., SF4, XeF4, ClF3, IF5).
Visuals showing the specific molecular shapes (seesaw, T-shaped, square planar, square pyramidal).
student_actions: Select central atoms with 5 or 6 electron domains.
Add varying numbers of lone pairs to observe different molecular geometries.
Match the predicted molecular geometries to given molecular formulas.

scenes.brief_purpose: Connect VSEPR predictions to the structures of common, real-world molecules and reinforce the relationship between geometry and properties.
key_visuals: 3D models of various molecules (e.g., H2O, NH3, CH4, CO2, BF3, PCl5, SF6).
Each molecule displayed with its predicted VSEPR geometry.
Optional: brief notes on how geometry influences polarity or reactivity.
student_actions: Predict the VSEPR geometry for a given molecule.
Compare the prediction to the displayed 3D model.
Select molecules and confirm their geometries match VSEPR theory.
